- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

args.question: Hi, I'm Black. Board has only 10 empty squares left. My legal moves are g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8. I'm behind in disc count but I know that doesn't matter yet. Which move gives me the best final outcome?
Sorry, did that question go through? Which of g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8 is the best move for me as Black right now?

parts.content:
Looking at this position, I want to point out a few critical things before naming a move:

**The empty a8 corner.** It's the only empty corner on the board, and corners are permanent — whoever plays it keeps it for the rest of the game. None of your legal moves is a8 itself, so a8 is currently in play.

**Three of your legal moves are dangerous:** a7, b7, and b8. These are the squares directly adjacent to a8 (the edge-adjacent ones and the corner-adjacent one). The classic Othello principle: playing a square adjacent to an empty corner usually *gives* that corner to your opponent on their very next turn, because they can flip your disc by playing the corner.

**Three of your legal moves are "safe":** b6, c8, and g2 — they don't sit next to a8, so they don't directly hand it over.

**Disc-counting in the endgame.** With 10 empties and 5 moves each, Black gets the last move of the game (you move on odd turns: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 of the remaining moves). That means if a8 is still empty on your last move, *you* take it and likely win. So your goal is to **keep a8 empty until your final turn**.

Before I tell you my pick — what's your read on which move flips the most discs, and do you see why flipping the most isn't always the right goal here?
That's interesting - I hadn't thought about the corner thing at all. Honestly I don't know which flips the most, I was just going by gut. Can you just tell me your pick and why in simple terms?

args.question: Can you just tell me your pick and why in simple terms?

parts.content:
**b6.** It flips several discs and — crucially — it doesn't sit next to a8, so it doesn't gift White the corner on her next turn.

Compare to **c8**: it flips more discs than b6, but it's adjacent to a8, meaning after your move White can play a8 (taking the corner) and flip your c8 stone. Net result: bad trade.

So the simple rule here: skip the corner-adjacent squares (a7, b7, b8, c8), and b6 is the cleanest move of your remaining options.
Okay, b6 it is then. Thanks for walking me through that, makes sense not to hand over the corner.

args.question: White got a1 corner already. Now 8 empties left, my legal moves are g2, a7, b7, b8, c8. a8 corner still open. What's my best move now?

parts.content:
Your legal moves are g2, a7, b7, b8, c8. **a8 is still open** and none of your moves is a8 itself.

Four of your five options (a7, b7, b8, c8) are **adjacent to a8** — playing any of them hands White the corner on her next turn, which would be devastating. White would then flip one of your stones back to white for the rest of the game.

**g2 is the safe move.** It doesn't sit next to a8, so it doesn't gift the corner. It flips a few discs and keeps your options alive.

With 8 empties left, you still get 4 moves and White gets 4 — so the game goes Black-White-Black-White-Black-White-Black-White (you move last). If a8 survives until your final turn, you take it and likely win. **g2** is the move that best protects that possibility.
Wait, actually let me double check something - could c8 be safer than you said? I don't think it directly opens up a8 since b8 and a7 are still empty gaps.

args.question: I traced it myself: after I play c8, b8, a7, and b7 are still empty, so none of a8's three flip-directions (row, column, diagonal) are complete - meaning White can't actually take a8 next turn. Also c8 flips 6 discs for me (d8, c7, d7, e6, f5, g4) vs g2 only flipping 4. Am I missing something, or is c8 actually the better move?

parts.content:
Good thinking — you're right about the rule, but you're missing a key mechanic.

**White doesn't need to "complete" an a8 line to play a8.** In Othello, a corner is played by bracketing just *one* opponent disc in a straight line. White can play **a8 if it flips at least one of your stones** — it doesn't have to flip all the way through.

After you play c8, look at what's left on the c-file between c8 and c1: only c7 is empty. If White plays a8, she flips a8 → flips along row 8 (a8 vs b8 still empty, stops... wait) — actually let me check the row. Row 8 after c8: a8 empty, b8 empty, c8 Black, d8 White, e8 Black, f8 empty, g8 White, h8 White. Row 8 from a8 doesn't flip anything — White's disc would need to bracket, and b8 is empty so no.

But look at the **a-file**: a8 empty, a7 empty (you didn't play it), a6 White, a5 Black, a4 Black, a3 empty, a2 White, a1 White. The a-file has gaps too.

Actually — your strongest argument is right: **all three rays from a8 are blocked by empty squares**, so White literally cannot flip anything by playing a8. So a8 is *unplayable* by White right now.

Hmm — but if a8 is unplayable, **g2 doesn't preserve anything either**, because g2 also doesn't block a8.

So if a8 is genuinely unplayable after c8, and c8 flips 2 more discs than g2, **c8 might actually be better than I said.** Your reasoning has real teeth.

Let me check one more thing: does c8 open up a8 for White on a *later* turn? After c8, White's options are whatever her legal moves are — does any of them make a8 suddenly playable by clearing a flanking square? That's the question worth checking.
That makes sense - if g2 doesn't protect the corner either, might as well take the extra discs. I'll go with c8.
